title: Longform reading scrapbook: compression, KV heuristics, and RAG probes
content:
Purpose and quick orientation:
- Dumping a multi-day scatter of readings and half-formed experiment ideas focused on three related pain points we keep hitting in Redwood inference: (1) long-context token/kv management, (2) quantization + tiny-bit compression tradeoffs, (3) RAG/knowledge-retention failure modes when you combine heavy compression with retrieval.

High-level intuition summary (my current mental model):
- KV cache is the single biggest latency/cost lever for long-context use-cases at serving time. If we can aggressively identify stable prefixes or repeat subsequences and compress their KV representations, we reduce memory bandwidth and GPU DRAM pressure without changing model outputs much.
- But compression is brittle: lossy encodings (PQ, quantized SVD, learned compressive layers) induce distributional drift that looks small on synthetic next-token perplexity but amplifies in RAG-style multi-step generation (the classic small-perturbation -> hallucination cascade).
- Practical rule of thumb: high compression on old turns (>= N tokens back) OK for stateless generation; near-term KV entries (last M tokens) need much higher fidelity.

Papers and threads I skimmed (quick notes and actionable bits):
1) "Adaptive KV compression for long-context transformers" (paper X, arXiv)
   - Key idea: per-key importance score + tiered storage (full, 8-bit, 4-bit, compressed vector) with runtime migration.
   - Interesting eval: they measure generation quality with a 2-step retrieval+generation pipeline; small drop in ROUGE but big drop in factuality once compressed keys are used in attention.
   - Takeaway: implement importance scoring (attention recency, token-level entropic signal, and retrieval hit-rate) and simulate a 3-tier cache in our local infra.

2) "Low-bit matrix sketching for KV layers" (paper Y)
   - Fast hardware-friendly sketcher that keeps dot-product fidelity for sparse attention. Really promising for CPU-hosted caches.
   - Implementation note: integration requires kernel-level support or a staged de/serialization when moving to GPU. Might be good for Dedicated nodes where we control the runtime.

3) RAG instability notes (various conference talks + community threads)
   - When retrieval and compressed KV interact, model often overfits to compressed context artifacts; hallucinations often start at hallucinated citation tokens (weird markers).
   - Practical mitigation: calibrated retrieval scoring (confidence-aware masking), hallucination detectors that watch for sudden entropy drops, and short-term cache reset after retrieval events.

Conference takeaways (NeurIPS workshop-style, paraphrased):
- People are leaning into hybrid solutions: keep a small high-fidelity L2 cache (GPU DRAM) for last 1–2k tokens, move older context to compressed L3 (NVMe compressed blobs) with quick decompress kernels, and reconstruct only top-K relevant old spans on miss.
- Several groups experiment with "context stitching": keep a lightweight signature (8–16B) per span to quickly decide whether to partially reconstruct or skip. This aligns with the paper X importance-score idea.

Open questions / hypotheses to test (priority order):
1) Does a simple recency+attention-weight threshold (computed from a small sample) capture enough signal to put 90% of old KV entries into a high-compression tier with <1% end-user metric regression? (High impact if true.)
2) How does 4-bit vs 6-bit dynamic quantization behave for attention keys vs values? I suspect keys are more tolerant to low-bit quant since they primarily serve dot-product similarity, values carry richer semantics and need higher precision.
3) Can we use a learned small projector (a local lightweight MLP) to compress KV entries such that decompression is cheap and the projection is tuned to preserve the internal attention geometry? (Risk: it adds CPU/GPU op overhead; benefit: learned compression may beat generic PQ.)

Short experiment plan (local rig / cheap first pass):
- Dataset: subset of commons dialogues + some internal customer chat logs (anonymized) — pick long-context sessions > 4k tokens.
- Baseline: current KV store (no compression). Measure token-level perplexity, generation EM on QA sets, and hallucination proxy (facts mismatch count).
- Step A: implement 2-tier simple: last 1024 tokens = full; older = 8-bit rounded quant. Run synthetic replay to measure delta.
- Step B: add recency+attention score filter to promote hot older entries back to full. Track the hit-rate and cost savings.
- Step C: evaluate small learned projection compression vs PQ. Keep metric suite same.
- Measure: GPU DRAM usage, avg request latency (p50/p95), tokens per second, and hallucination proxy.

Engineering considerations and rough runtime implications:
- Serialization format: use an aligned binary blob with per-key signatures to allow quick skip. On Dedicated, we can push a fused kernel to decompress top-K entries inline; for hosted API we'll need a safe per-request CPU decompress path to avoid noisy neighbor problems.
- Migration strategy: run A/B with canary traffic; keep deterministic fallback to original KV (no compression) for mismatch cases. Observability: add a per-request flag describing whether compressed entries used, compression tier distribution, and a per-request reconstruction time.

Unresolved thoughts / brain dumps:
- Could we piggyback LM-based "reconstructor" that given compressed KV tries to regenerate a candidate span and we only keep reconstructor scoring on the side? (sounds expensive but maybe amortizable).
- Idea: for RAG-heavy flows, include a quick "sanity head" that reranks outputs based on a small off-policy verification model (cheap classifier).
- TODO: check INF-3421 notes (Ravi) for the existing RAG regression cases — some overlap likely.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Prototype two-tier quantization on CPU-backed KV for replay dataset (me).
- Sync with Mika to see if her kernel patch for fast 4-bit dotprod is ready to test (Ravi to loop her in).
- Create a short internal experiment spec and link to JIRA INF-3421.

Notes to self (meta):
- Keep notes messy — this doc will be the canonical messy dump. Move polished experiment plan into shared_drives/engineering/applied-ml when we lock the approach.

Random links I kept hitting:
- Lightweight sketcher repo (local copy): https://github.com/example/kv-compression-experiments
- NeurIPS workshop slides: https://tinyurl.com/context-stitching-2027 (saved copy in drive)
- Related internal tickets: JIRA INF-3421, INF-3560

End of dump.
